Rotten
ROT-n
adj.
From rot, Saxon rotian, to putrefy. Webster 1828: putrid; decayed; carious; unsound. Scripture uses it of a garment consumed by moths, of seed under the clods, and of the rags that saved a prophet’s life.

Biblical Definition

Rotten in Scripture is decay from within, and it is used both of judgment and, once, of a great kindness. Job uses it of man’s frame under God’s hand: And he, as a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten (Job 13:28) — not struck down but consumed slowly, the way cloth goes. Joel uses it of a harvest failing before it starts: The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered (Joel 1:17). Nothing had been harvested badly; nothing had come up. And Jeremiah 38 supplies one of the most touching details in the Old Testament. Jeremiah had been let down with cords into a dungeon of mire, and Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a foreign servant in a hostile court, obtained the king’s leave to pull him out: Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:11) — and told him to put them under his armholes so the cords would not cut him. A rescue conducted with rotten rags, and the care of it recorded for ever.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ROTTEN as putrid; decayed; carious; unsound; and figuratively, corrupt, treacherous, or not to be trusted.

expand to see more

ROTTEN, a. — Putrid; decayed; carious; having the natural texture destroyed by decomposition.

Not firm or trusty; unsound; defective in substance; as, rotten timber.

Figuratively, corrupt; treacherous; deceitful; as, a rotten heart or a rotten cause.

Applied to seed that perishes in the ground, and to garments consumed by the moth.

From Saxon rotian, to putrefy — the root also of rot and rottenness.

Key Scripture

Job 13:28 — "And he, as a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten."

Joel 1:17 — "The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered."

Jeremiah 38:11 — "So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah."

Proverbs 13:5 — "A righteous man hateth lying: but a wicked man is loathsome, and cometh to shame."

Modern Corruption

Ebedmelech, a foreign eunuch in a collapsing court, is the man who acted while the officials of God’s own people left a prophet to sink in mud, and Scripture records his reward by name.

expand to see more

The princes had told Zedekiah that Jeremiah weakeneth the hands of the men of war, and the weak king answered, Behold, he is in your hand: for the king is not he that can do any thing against you. They put the prophet in a cistern with no water and much mire. Then Ebedmelech — an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a foreigner with no standing in Israel’s covenant and everything to lose — went to the king in the gate of Benjamin, told him plainly that the men had done evil, and got thirty men and a rope. God sent him a personal word by Jeremiah afterwards: I will deliver thee… because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD (Jeremiah 39:18). The dictionary notes what this pattern means for the church: when God’s people fail, He is not without a servant, and He often raises one from outside the expected circle.

Job 13:28 and Joel 1:17 supply the other and sombre use, and both refuse the modern preference for sudden catastrophe over slow decay. Job says man is consumed as a rotten thing… as a garment that is moth eaten — a wasting nobody watches, which is how most lives actually end. Joel says the seed rotted under the clods, so that the failure had already happened before anyone could see a field. Sin works the same way in a soul and in a congregation: not by a single visible collapse but by a quiet rotting under the surface while the barns still stand. That is why Scripture’s remedy is repeated self-examination, and why Joel’s response to the ruined harvest was a called assembly rather than an inquest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew raqab (H7538), rottenness, decay; abash (H5685), to shrivel, to rot; machaq, to decay; Greek sapros (G4550), rotten, corrupt, worthless.

expand to see more

Hebrew raqab (H7538) — rottenness, decay; envy the rottenness of the bones (Proverbs 14:30).

Hebrew abash (H5685) — to shrivel, to rot; the seed is rotten under their clods (Joel 1:17).

Hebrew rakab — the verbal root, to rot; used of a name that rots (Proverbs 10:7).

Greek sapros (G4550) — rotten, putrid, worthless; let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth (Ephesians 4:29).

Greek ses (G4597) — a moth; where moth and rust doth corrupt (Matthew 6:19).

Usage

"As a rotten thing, consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten (Job 13:28) — a wasting nobody watches."

"The seed is rotten under their clods (Joel 1:17) — the failure complete before a field could show it."

"Old cast clouts and old rotten rags (Jeremiah 38:11) — a rescue conducted with refuse, and recorded for ever."
